title: Hair's breadth
hook: the poem: a hair's breadth of difference and heaven and earth are set apart

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Xinxin Ming, faith in mind: the great way is not difficult, for those who don't pick and choose. Your line: no picking and choosing. Which preference did you set down? Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

A ship leaves harbor with its wheel turned the smallest bit off true. From the dock, nobody could see it. A day out, the coast still looks right. But keep sailing, across a whole ocean, and that ship comes ashore on a different coast from the one it meant to reach. The turn was tiny. The distance it opens is not. The poem we started yesterday has a line built on exactly this shape, the smallest possible gap and the largest possible distance. Today: a hair's breadth.
screen: `A SHIP LEAVES HARBOR.` → `THE WHEEL, A HAIR OFF TRUE.` → `A DIFFERENT COAST.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. In paraphrase, the Xinxin Ming says: if there is the slightest difference, a hair's breadth, then heaven and earth are set apart. It comes only a few lines after the opening we heard yesterday, so it is not a new subject. It is the same warning about picking and choosing, now with a picture of how big the cost can grow. Second, what the line is not. It can sound like a call to be exacting, to get every detail perfect, a hair's breadth off and you've failed. But that reading turns the line into one more round of picking and choosing: right against wrong, perfect against flawed. The difference the poem means is the split the mind makes between what is here and what it wants instead. Third, where that split opens. It's usually very small. A name lights up on your phone and, before you read a word, there's a flicker. Ugh. Or a flicker of yes, this one I like. No story yet, no argument, just a lean. That lean is the hair's breadth. Fourth, why heaven and earth. The poem pairs the smallest thing it can name with the largest. It isn't threatening anyone. It's describing distance. A tiny lean, held and fed, tilts the whole conversation, then the whole relationship, the way a hair off on the wheel puts a ship on another coast. And the same line has a gentler side. If the gap begins as a hair, it can also be noticed while it is still only a hair wide.
screen: `THE LINE: A HAIR'S BREADTH.` · `NOT A CALL TO BE PERFECT.` · `THE FIRST FLICKER OF A LEAN.` · `SMALLEST THING, LARGEST DISTANCE.` · then, large: `A HAIR'S BREADTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and let the breath settle into its own rhythm. Let sounds, thoughts and sensations come as they come. Watch for the very first flicker as each one arrives: a slight lean toward it, or a slight lean away. Before any story. When you catch one, you can name it quietly: lean. Then let it pass. Near the end, bring to mind one small bias you carry, the coworker whose messages you skim, the voice you tune out a little early. Just see it, a hair wide. The bell holds the time.
Hair's breadth. In the Xinxin Ming, the slightest difference, the tiny lean of liking and disliking, which sets heaven and earth apart. Today's word.
Your line: a hair's breadth. Today, catch one small bias while it is still only a flicker, before it becomes a story. Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Zen and Chan teachers often quote this line of the Xinxin Ming in talks to point at how quickly a small preference becomes a large separation, and students use it as a reminder during sitting.

original.note: Chinese (haoli): 'a hair's breadth', the smallest gap, set against heaven and earth in the poem's line.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hair's breadth just means a near miss.
what it means: the tiniest lean of liking or disliking, which in the poem sets heaven and earth apart.
what a scholar hears: the line sets the smallest thing it can name beside the largest, heaven and earth, to describe distance rather than punishment.
